passage:
Saturday. At the school fair, Pranav held up a phone to show everyone the painting and first-prize certificate of Pranav's daughter Vidya. "Did you see her maths marks too?" Pranav asked a neighbour. Vidya tugged Pranav's sleeve, cheeks red.

Tuesday. At dinner Vidya said, "You only clap when I win." Pranav paused, fork in the air. "That's not true." Then the fair came back to mind. "Tell me one thing you did this week that you're proud of." Vidya said, "I helped Meera when she fell, and I kept trying the hard puzzle even when it was annoying."

Sunday. Pranav asked to see the unfinished puzzle. "You kept at it. I love watching you try." Vidya beamed. Pranav had once dreamed of being a painter and, this time, didn't say a word about brushes.

qa.q: What did Pranav show everyone at the school fair?
qa.a: Pranav showed everyone Vidya's painting and first-prize certificate.

qa.q: Why did Vidya tug Pranav's sleeve with red cheeks?
qa.a: Vidya seems embarrassed by the showing off, and later says 'You only clap when I win,' suggesting feeling valued for results.

qa.q: What did Pranav change after Tuesday's dinner?
qa.a: Pranav asked what Vidya was proud of and began praising effort, like keeping at the puzzle and helping Meera, rather than prizes.

qa.q: How might Pranav have felt when Vidya said, "You only clap when I win"?
qa.a: Pranav seemed caught off guard, pausing with the fork in the air and denying it, before remembering the fair and changing how Pranav praised Vidya.

grounding: A parent proud of their child shifts praise from marks and prizes to effort and character and keeps their own unfulfilled dreams out of it.
